intro: Ives crowds seven themes onto the first page of his portrait of Emerson, then spends the movement letting them speak. Beethoven’s four-note knock keeps breaking into the piano’s argument.

cues.title: Seven themes crowd the page
cues.text: Seven themes crowd the opening page, some only a few notes long. They interrupt and overlap in the piano, including scraps of the melody that will sing so plainly in The Alcotts. Ives begins in the middle of the argument.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Emerson”: seven overlapping themes on the first page and fragments of the cyclic melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two hundred unexpected parcels
cues.text: In January 1921 Ives mails two hundred copies of the Concord Sonata to people in the music world. He has paid for the printing himself. An insurance executive’s enormous piano sonata arrives on their desks, accompanied by a book of essays.
cues.evidence: Gann’s introductory account and chronology: printing at Ives’s expense in 1920, score and essays circulated in January 1921. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Emerson and the crowd
cues.text: Behind this piano movement stands an unfinished concerto from 1910–11. Ives casts the soloist as Emerson and the orchestra as the crowd answering him. The sonata brings both sides of that exchange under one pianist’s hands.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: the unfinished Emerson Concerto and Ives’s conception of the soloist and responding masses. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: A verse among the speeches
cues.text: A quiet lyrical theme makes room in the piano’s argument. Ives calls it verse in the score: Emerson’s poetry beside his prose. The tune leads towards an apparent restart and then a large Beethoven-based climax.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, third episode and Example 3: the score’s verse label and the subsequent false return and Beethoven climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Downward tune, upward bass
cues.text: A high melody descends while figures rise beneath it in the bass. The melody comes round repeatedly, gaining notes and thicker chords each time. This middle episode begins and ends softly, with its great swell between.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, central episode on score pp. 8–11 and Example 4: descending melody, rising lower patterns and progressive enlargement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song starts to multiply
cues.text: The Emerson theme returns in a delicate, song-like passage. Then the piano grows busy with fugue-like entries, largely drawn from the earlier verse theme. One line begins before another has finished.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: song-like episode after the centre, followed by fugue-like writing based largely on the verse theme. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A score still changing
cues.text: Ives starts revising the sonata by 1921, with Emerson receiving particular attention. A substantially revised edition reaches print in 1947. For more than twenty years after mailing the score, he is still changing the notes.
cues.evidence: Gann’s chronology: revisions from 1921 and the new edition in print in 1947 (second edition, Arrow Music Press, later Associated Music Publishers). The recording source does not specify an edition. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Old phrases, another outburst
cues.text: Music from the opening episodes returns. Beethoven’s repeated-note figure again drives towards a C minor climax, answering the great outburst in the movement’s first third.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: late recapitulation starting with the first episode, and the two large C minor Beethoven-based climaxes. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The knock grows distant
cues.text: The Emerson theme breaks into pieces. Beethoven’s four-note figure echoes in A major and E♭ major, keys a tritone apart. At the end, the knock survives as a slow, dark phrase in the bass.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, closing paragraph: dismantled Emerson theme, Beethoven echoes in A major and E♭ major, and the final bass statement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A quiet verse emerges
transitions.from: Intro · Seven themes crowd the piano
transitions.to: A · A quiet verse for piano
transitions.how: The overlapping piano phrases make room for a quiet lyrical theme, labelled verse. Its clear upper line begins another episode, which eventually grows into the first great C minor outburst on Beethoven’s repeated-note figure.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, third episode and Example 3: verse theme, false return and Beethoven climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: A high tune above rising figures
transitions.from: B · Beethoven among the piano chords
transitions.to: C · A high melody, rising bass
transitions.how: After the Beethoven climax, a descending melody starts quietly high in the piano. Rising bass figures move beneath it. The melody repeats with added notes and thicker chords, building a long arch that will end softly as it began.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, central episode, score pp. 8–11 and Example 4. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The Emerson tune sings again
transitions.from: C · A high melody, rising bass
transitions.to: D · A song becomes a fugue
transitions.how: The repeated high melody subsides. A delicate song-like version of the Emerson theme follows in the piano, then the earlier verse theme supplies much of the fugue-like writing. The new lines pick up tunes already heard among the louder chords.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: central episode, subsequent Emerson-theme song and verse-theme fugue. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: C minor breaks into distant echoes
transitions.to: Coda · Beethoven echoes in distant keys
transitions.how: The later Beethoven climax in C minor begins to dissolve. The Emerson tune breaks apart, while the repeated-note figure sounds in A major and E♭ major. These distant echoes grow quieter until the piano’s bass is left with the slow final statement.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, closing account: the second C minor climax and the distant-key echoes that follow it. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: He sold life insurance in New York and wrote music in which a hymn across the river could outlast a whole marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut. Charles, born there in 1874, grew up with a father for whom a wrong note could be the beginning of an experiment.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, putting the tune of God Save the King through a teenager’s display of keyboard tricks. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and how to sustain a symphony. His First Symphony was the result: a young American speaking fluent European. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term. His son kept talking about him for the next sixty years.
